title: Proximal-IMH: Proximal Posterior Proposals for Independent Metropolis–Hastings with Approximate Operators
topic: Probabilistic Methods->Monte Carlo and Sampling Methods
claim: Our proximal correction keeps divergence from the exact target orders of magnitude lower than baselines across noise, operator error, observation ratio, and dimension.
layout: 2x2 grid of log-log line plots, shared top legend, rotated label tags
description: A 2x2 grid of line plots under a shared rounded legend box. The legend names three methods: Approx (green), Latent (blue) and Proximal (pink). Each panel plots KL divergence on a log y-axis against a different variable. Top left is noise level (log10 SNR), top right is operator error (relative norm of A minus its approximation, in percent), bottom left is observation ratio (dy/d, in percent), and bottom right is dimension d. Each panel has a rotated grey rounded label tag on its left edge. In every panel the pink Proximal curve sits about two to three orders of magnitude below the green and blue curves, and it rises only slowly. Approx and Latent grow with operator error and dimension. Latent stays flat against noise and observation ratio. The eye goes first to the wide gap between the pink line and the other two.
caption: Sensitivity of the expected KL divergence of the Approx, Latent, and Proximal proposals (relative to the \Exact) for different noise levels, operator errors, observation ratios, and dimensions. Details of the experimental setup are given in [ref].
abstract: We consider the problem of sampling from a posterior distribution arising in Bayesian inverse problems in science, engineering, and imaging. Our method belongs to the family of independence Metropolis-Hastings (IMH) sampling algorithms, which are common in Bayesian inference. Relying on the existence of an approximate posterior distribution that is cheaper to sample from but may have significant bias, we introduce Proximal-IMH, a scheme that removes this bias by correcting samples from the approximate posterior through an auxiliary optimization problem. This yields a local adjustment that trades off adherence to the exact model against stability around the approximate reference point. For idealized settings, we prove that the proximal correction tightens the match between approximate and exact posteriors, thereby improving acceptance rates and mixing. The method applies to both linear and nonlinear input-output operators and is particularly suitable for inverse problems where exact posterior sampling is too expensive. We present numerical experiments including multimodal and data-driven priors with nonlinear input-output operators. The results show that Proximal-IMH reliably outperforms existing IMH variants.
